opus-5.5.text:
I think forgetting is probably the single most important ingredient that made linear attention actually competitive. If you go back to the original linear attention formulation, you can view it as a recurrent model where the hidden state is a matrix, and at every step you just add the outer product of the key and value into that state. The problem is that it only ever adds. There's no way to remove anything. So as the sequence gets longer, the state keeps accumulating information, and since it has a fixed size, everything starts interfering with everything else. You get this kind of memory collision, and the model's retrieval quality degrades badly.

Forgetting, or gating, gives the model a way to decay old information. That idea is actually very old. It's what made LSTMs work so much better than vanilla RNNs, because the forget gate lets the network decide what to keep and what to throw away. In the linear attention world, the first step was something like a fixed decay, as in RetNet, where you multiply the state by a constant less than one at every step. That already helps a lot because it gives a recency bias. But a fixed decay is data-independent, so the model can't choose to remember something important for a long time while discarding noise quickly.

The bigger improvement came from data-dependent gating, as in Mamba, GLA, and later models, where the decay rate is a function of the current input. Then the model can say, at this token I want to clear my memory, and at this other token I want to hold onto everything. That selectivity turns out to be crucial, especially for language modeling.

I'd also point out that gating is just one way of managing memory. Another line is the delta rule, as in DeltaNet, where instead of only decaying the whole state, you do a targeted update: you first retrieve what the memory currently associates with a key, and then you correct it toward the new value. That's more like overwriting a specific slot than fading everything uniformly. What we found in Gated DeltaNet is that these two mechanisms are complementary. Gating gives you fast, coarse-grained forgetting, like wiping memory when the context switches, and the delta rule gives you precise, fine-grained edits. Combining them works better than either alone.

So in my view, the evolution of linear attention is largely the story of learning how to manage a finite memory well. Transformers sidestep the problem by keeping everything in the KV cache, which is costly but lossless. Linear models have to compress, and once you compress, deciding what to forget becomes just as important as deciding what to remember.

r001.rationale: It says performance degrades as sequences get longer, but does not state that early linear attention performed poorly even on short texts.

r002.rationale: It does not mention ReLA or credit its forgetting-decay mechanism with good language-modeling performance at scale.

r003.rationale: It does not mention Mamba2 or characterize it as linear attention with decay.

r004.rationale: It explains that data-dependent gating makes decay depend on the current input, allowing the model to choose what to clear and what to retain.

fable-5.1.text:
I think forgetting is really the thing that made linear attention go from an interesting idea to something that actually works at scale.

If you look at the original linear attention from 2020, it's basically a recurrent state that just keeps accumulating key-value outer products. Every token you see gets added to the state, and nothing ever gets removed. The problem is that the state has a fixed size, so you're trying to compress an ever-growing history into a fixed-capacity memory. Without any way to discard information, the memory saturates, old and new information interfere with each other, and retrieval gets noisy. Softmax attention doesn't have this problem because it keeps the whole KV cache around and can look anything up exactly. So linear attention was always going to lose on recall unless it learned to manage its memory.

Forgetting is that management mechanism. Once you add a decay term, the model can decide how much of the old state to keep versus how much to overwrite with new content. The first versions of this were data-independent, things like the fixed exponential decay in RetNet, or the positional decay in RWKV-4. Those already helped a lot because they impose a recency bias, which is a good prior for language. But the big jump came with data-dependent gating. In Mamba, in GLA, in RWKV-6 and later, the forget gate is computed from the input, so the model can hold onto something for a long time when it's important and flush the state quickly when the context shifts. That's really the point: forgetting lets the model allocate its limited memory selectively rather than uniformly.

There's also a nice way to see it from the perspective of the recurrence itself. If you write the state update as S_t = G_t ⊙ S_{t-1} + v_t k_t^T, then without the gate G_t you just have a sum, which is a very weak form of memory. With the gate, you have a controlled dynamical system. And when you push this further, towards things like DeltaNet or Gated DeltaNet, the forgetting becomes even more structured. Instead of decaying the whole state by a scalar, you selectively erase the part of memory associated with the current key before writing the new value. That's forgetting in a more targeted sense, like a key-specific overwrite instead of a global fade. In my experience that combination, a global gate plus a targeted delta-rule update, is what gives you both good long-context stability and good in-context retrieval.

So I'd say the role of forgetting is twofold. Practically, it fixes the memory saturation problem and closes much of the gap with softmax attention on language modeling. Conceptually, it reframes linear attention as a learned memory system with explicit write and erase operations, rather than a cheap approximation of softmax. Once you think of it that way, a lot of the recent progress, better gating parameterizations, delta rules, state-size scaling, all fits into one picture: it's about teaching the model what to keep and what to let go.

astra-6.text:
I think forgetting is a key part of making linear attention more effective. In linear attention, you typically compress the history into a fixed-size state. As new information comes in, you keep updating that state. But if you only accumulate information, older content can interfere with what matters now.

A forgetting mechanism lets the model control what it retains. The simplest version applies a fixed decay: recent information gets more weight, and older information gradually fades. A more flexible version makes that decay depend on the input, so the model can preserve information that remains useful and discard information when the context changes.

What matters is that forgetting also changes how you write to memory. If you want to store something new, it helps to remove outdated information first. Otherwise, you’re asking a limited state to represent everything at once.

So I would view forgetting as a way to manage memory, rather than just a preference for recent tokens. The challenge is to make that management selective enough to improve the model’s expressiveness while preserving the computational efficiency that makes linear attention attractive.

sol-6.1.text:
I think forgetting is fundamentally about deciding which parts of the past should remain useful. In linear attention, we compress the history into a fixed-size state. That makes computation efficient, but it also means that old information and new information have to share limited capacity. If we keep adding information without selectively removing anything, the state can become crowded, and irrelevant context can interfere with what we need now.

A forgetting mechanism gives the model a way to manage that state. Instead of simply accumulating everything, it can decay or overwrite information as new inputs arrive. A fixed decay introduces a preference for recent information; an input-dependent gate can make that decision more selective, retaining something important even when it occurred much earlier.

The challenge is to make forgetting expressive while preserving the efficient computation that motivates linear attention. Too much forgetting loses long-range dependencies; too little allows interference to build up. So I would view forgetting as a form of memory management: the goal is to retain the right information for the task, rather than retain as much as possible.
